archetype.name: Pretender (trench-depleted)
archetype.definition: A .500 team whose underlying play ranks near the bottom of the league. Two field-goal-margin wins hide a -8 per-game point differential, a broken run game and a defense that cannot get off the field.

report.headline: A 2-2 record built on two 3-point escapes; the play says bottom-five.
report.take:
Green Bay is 2-2, but nothing else about the season looks like a .500 team. Net EPA ranks 30th. The point differential is -32 through four games. The two wins came by three points each, against the Jets and a Tampa Bay offense that now ranks 32nd. The two losses came by 17 and 21. The Packers are 0-3-1 against the spread, so they have not beaten expectations once. Measured against the last two seasons, when the offense ranked 8th and 4th in EPA, this is a sharp drop. It is not a continuation.

The drop starts up front. The rushing offense is last in the league by EPA (-0.406 per play) and 31st in stuff rate. Backs average 1.75 yards before contact, and the line ranks 29th in pressure allowed and dead last with 33 QB hits allowed. Jordan Love is getting the ball out in 2.48 seconds, 31st in time to throw. That reads as self-defense, not a scheme choice. Add 10.5 penalties a game (31st), 5.5 of them on the line, and drives keep dying behind the chains. The result is 26.8 minutes of possession per game, 31st, which leaves an already shaky defense on the field.

The numbers do hide some good news. The passing game is roughly league-average (15th in EPA) and has improved every week. Love's pass EPA went from -2.7 and -3.2 in the first two games to +3.6 and +6.9 in the last two, despite losing Jayden Reed to IR. The defense has allowed explosive passes at the 4th-lowest rate and has 10 sacks (8th) without Micah Parsons playing a snap. Its failures are about sustained drives: 48.2% on third down (29th) and touchdowns on 85.7% of red-zone trips (32nd). That is a fixable, high-variance profile more than proof of a bad unit.

The direction depends on bodies, and the injury list is getting worse faster than it is getting better. Starting center Jacob Monk (96% of snaps) and guard Aaron Banks are out, with tackle Zach Bako-Bewele already on IR. Edgerrin Cooper, an 83%-snap linebacker, tore his Achilles in the Tampa win. Two interior defensive linemen are also out. Parsons' estimated return around Week 6 is the biggest positive swing on the board. The schedule does turn generous on offense: Dallas, Detroit twice, New Orleans, Buffalo, Miami and Houston all rank 25th or worse in defensive EPA. Several of those teams can also score, though, and this defense has not shown it can stop sustained drives.

strengths.title: Passing game trending the right way
strengths.body: The pass offense ranks 15th in EPA even with a line under constant pressure. Love's per-game pass EPA has climbed from negative in Weeks 1-2 to strongly positive in Weeks 3-4. Matthew Golden (37 targets), Christian Watson (32) and Tucker Kraft (24) give him a stable top three. Love's track record suggests this is closer to his true level than the early games were, provided the protection does not collapse further.

strengths.title: Pass defense limits the big play
strengths.body: The defense allows explosive passes at the 4th-lowest rate. It has 10 sacks (8th) and sacks the quarterback on 7.1% of dropbacks (11th), all without Parsons. The coverage shell is keeping things in front of it. If Parsons returns on schedule, the pass rush has room to rise from good to disruptive.

strengths.title: Special teams adding real value
strengths.body: Special teams are worth 1.79 EPA per game, 10th in the league. That kind of margin matters for a team whose two wins came by a field goal. It is a modest, fairly stable edge rather than a driver.

concerns.title: Offensive line and run game collapsing
concerns.body: The run game is the worst in football by EPA and second-worst by stuff rate. Backs barely get past the line before contact. This is a line problem, not a back problem: three different runners have similar results. It is getting worse, with the starting center and a guard out and a tackle on IR. The line also allows the most QB hits in the league.

concerns.title: Defense cannot finish drives
concerns.body: Opponents convert 48.2% of third downs (29th) and score touchdowns on 85.7% of red-zone trips (32nd). Atlanta ran for 242 yards. The run front is now without Cooper and two interior linemen, so the early-down run defense is likely to get worse before Parsons helps. Red-zone rates tend to regress toward average, but the personnel losses argue against much relief soon.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted penalties
concerns.body: At 10.5 penalties per game (31st), with 5.5 on the line, Green Bay keeps putting itself in long-yardage spots its run game cannot escape. The Jets game alone cost 133 penalty yards. Discipline is coachable, but a reshuffled line with backups tends to draw more flags, not fewer.

trend.note: Results have alternated: blowout loss, field-goal win, blowout loss, field-goal win, with 39, 17, 35 and 14 points allowed. The one steady thread is the passing game, which has improved every week while the run game stayed negative throughout.

nextGame.headline: A depleted Packers line meets one of the league's best pass rushes
nextGame.body:
Chicago is the profile Green Bay least wants to see right now. The Bears rank 4th in net EPA, 2nd against the pass and 3rd in pressure rate. They hold teams to 23.7% on third down, and they control the clock better than anyone at 36.6 minutes per game. Their soft spots are real: 27th in run defense EPA and 28th in deep-pass EPA allowed. Green Bay is poorly built to exploit either one. Its run game is last in the league, and its quick-release passing rarely gets time to push the ball downfield. On the other side, the Bears' run game (4.75 yards per carry, 6th in yards before contact) runs straight at a defense that just lost Cooper and two interior linemen.

Availability cuts both ways. Chicago is without Caleb Williams, so Case Keenum makes his third straight start. The Bears are also missing corners Cam Lewis and Kyler Gordon, safety Anthony Johnson Jr. and left tackle Braxton Jones. That secondary is thin enough to make the deep-ball weakness real. Green Bay is missing center Jacob Monk and guard Aaron Banks against an elite rush. Cooper is gone for the year, Parsons is not expected back until next week, and starting corner Brandon Cisse is questionable with a neck injury. The Packers are home 3-point underdogs, which tells you how far the market has moved on them.

keyMatchups.title: Bears rush vs. makeshift interior line
keyMatchups.body: Chicago pressures at the 3rd-highest rate and sacks at the 4th-highest. Green Bay already allows the 29th-highest pressure rate, and now loses its starting center and a guard. If Love cannot hold up long enough even for his short game, drives stall before the passing game can matter.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots at a thinned secondary
keyMatchups.body: Chicago is elite against short passes (2nd) but 28th on deep throws. It is now missing two corners and a safety. This is Green Bay's clearest path to points, through Golden and Watson. It only works if protection survives long enough to let those routes develop.

keyMatchups.title: Bears ground game, Packers' clock
keyMatchups.body: With Keenum at quarterback, Chicago has every reason to lean on a run game averaging 4.75 yards per carry against a front missing Cooper. The Bears' time-of-possession edge against Green Bay's 31st-ranked mark could shrink the Packers' possessions to a handful.

nextGame.watch: Green Bay's interior line on early downs: how often Love is hit inside three seconds decides whether the Bears' deep-coverage holes ever come into play.

restOfSeason.body:
Some regression should help Green Bay. A red-zone touchdown rate allowed of 85.7% is unlikely to hold, and the schedule is loaded with bottom-ten defenses that should lift an offense whose passing is already league-average. Parsons' return would be the single biggest upgrade available. But the run game and the line are the structural problem, and the line is losing starters, not getting them back. Until the interior stabilizes, expect an offense that moves the ball through the air in spurts and stalls in short yardage.

The close-game record is what should regress. Being 2-0 in one-score games with a -8 point differential is not a foundation. Many of the soft defenses ahead (Dallas, Detroit, Buffalo) belong to offenses ranked 6th or better, which will punish a defense that cannot get off the field. Realistically this looks like a team hovering around .500 that needs Parsons and a healthy line to get back into the playoff conversation of the last two years.
swingFactors: Health of the interior offensive line (Monk, Banks)

bets.reason: Green Bay has not topped 22 points in any game. It faces the No. 2 pass defense and No. 3 pressure unit without its starting center and a guard, and its run game ranks last in EPA. The Bears' clock control should also limit the Packers' possessions.

The net EPA gap is wide: Chicago 4th, Green Bay 30th. Chicago has covered 75% of its games against Green Bay's 0-3-1, and the Packers' injuries are concentrated where the Bears are strongest. Keenum starting instead of Williams keeps this from being stronger.

Averaging each side's scoring and points allowed lands near 44.5 before accounting for Williams' absence. Chicago likely leans on the run with Keenum, and both teams play to long possessions. Green Bay's leaky red-zone defense is the main risk to the under.
The home-dog price may tempt, but Green Bay's two wins were 3-point escapes against weak competition. Its EPA profile is bottom-three, and this matchup attacks its two biggest injury holes.

confidence.note: Four-game sample and heavy injury churn on both lines, plus Parsons' pending return, could reshape the profile quickly.
